column6: Older text, not fixed: q0 explanation blames BEAST on MAC-then-Encrypt padding oracles (BEAST was a predictable-IV CBC attack), and "eliminating composition errors entirely" overstates.

Belief "keeping the algorithm secret adds real protection" is arguably true (obscurity can add delay), so the bullet implied a false absolute; reworded belief to "is a sound basis for a cipher's security".

Pedersen exercise "in integers mod 23" fails for many choices: the trapdoor opening divides by log_g(h) mod 22, which is impossible when it is even or 11. Specified the order-11 subgroup generated by g = 2.
Each scheme makes one of them computational overstated; hash commitments (per the file's own Core Idea) make both computational. Now "at least one".

Belief "the reduction goes from the hard problem to the scheme" matches standard phrasing ("reduce DDH to breaking the scheme"), so it was not clearly false; restated the belief as the actual wrong direction (solver for the problem turned into an attack).

Toy scheme "message plus a multiple of a secret plus a small error" cannot be decrypted when worked: c mod p gives m + e and m cannot be separated. Replaced with the DGHV form c = m + 2e + pq, decrypt (c mod p) mod 2.
The good basis finds it easily and the bad one does not is an absolute a worked 2D example may not show (bad-basis rounding sometimes hits the nearest point). Softened to usually/often.
Belief lumped "random" with "repeated" CTR nonces; random nonces of adequate length are fine, and the correction only addressed repetition. Dropped "random or".
Any CA the browser trusts can issue for any domain is an absolute; browsers name-constrain some roots (e.g. to certain TLDs). Now "Most CAs".

Correction was circular ("factoring n is hard without knowing p and q") and placed security on finding d instead of the RSA problem (e-th roots). Rewrote belief and correction around the trapdoor and e-th roots, with factoring as an upper bound.
